title: In the shops
topic: buying clothes and objects; demonstratives; lequel; tout
why: After comparing things, you now learn to point at them and choose: this one, that one, which one, all of them. It's the vocabulary of clothes shopping in France, from the fitting room to the sales, and the last new point before the big A2 review.

In a clothes shop

Shopping for clothes in France follows a little ritual. You walk in and say Bonjour (always: entering a shop without greeting the staff sounds rude), the assistant asks Je peux vous aider ?, and you answer Oui, je cherche un pull or Non merci, je regarde. Then come the sizes, the fitting room and the checkout.

FrenchEnglish
Je peux l'essayer ?Can I try it on?
Où est la cabine d'essayage ?Where is the fitting room?
Vous faites quelle taille ? — Je fais du 38.What size are you? — I'm a 38.
Vous faites quelle pointure ? — Je fais du 42.What's your shoe size? — I'm a 42.
C'est trop grand / trop petit / trop serré.It's too big / too small / too tight.
Vous l'avez en bleu ? en 40 ? en plus grand ?Do you have it in blue? in a 40? in a bigger size?
Ça vous va très bien !It really suits you!
Je le prends.I'll take it.

Two words for “size”: la taille for clothes, la pointure for shoes. And notice Je fais du 38: French uses faire, where English uses “to be”. French sizes are not American sizes, so check the label.

Aller = to suit

You know aller for movement and for Ça va ?. With an indirect pronoun, it means “to suit, to fit”: Cette veste te va bien (this jacket suits you), Ces chaussures vous vont bien. The thing you wear is the subject, the person is me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Careful: Ça vous va ? can also mean “Is that OK for you?”, for a time or a price.

Les soldes (the sales) are always plural and masculine: les soldes d'hiver, in January, and les soldes d'été, in summer. Keep your ticket de caisse (receipt): you will need it to échanger (exchange) an item or to be remboursé (refunded).

", "

This one, that one, which one?

English has “this” and “that”. French has one demonstrative adjective that agrees with the noun, like an article. It does not say “near” or “far” by itself.

before a consonantbefore a vowel or silent h
masculinece pullcet article, cet homme
femininecette robecette écharpe
pluralces chaussuresces‿articles (liaison)

Cet and cette sound exactly the same. Ce pull can mean “this sweater” or “that sweater”: the context decides. To insist, add -ci (here) or -là (there): ce pull-ci, cette robe-là.

Celui-ci, celle-là

To avoid repeating the noun, use the pronoun, which also agrees: celui (masc.), celle (fem.), ceux (masc. plural), celles (fem. plural), followed by -ci or -là.

Quel manteau préférez-vous ? Celui-ci ou celui-là ?Which coat do you prefer? This one or that one?
Ces bottes sont trop petites. Je peux essayer celles-là ?These boots are too small. Can I try those ones?

In everyday speech, -là is used much more than -ci, even for something close: Je prends celui-là is simply “I'll take that one”.

Lequel ? Laquelle ?

“Which one?” is lequel (masc.), laquelle (fem.), lesquels, lesquelles: it's quel glued to the article, and it agrees with the noun you have in mind.

— J'adore cette jupe ! — Laquelle ? La rouge ?— I love this skirt! — Which one? The red one?

You will also hear the possessive pronouns: le mien, la mienne, les miens, les miennes (mine), le tien, la tienne (yours), le sien, la sienne (his or hers), le nôtre, le vôtre, le leur. Like mon / ma, they agree with the thing owned: C'est ton sac ? — Non, ce n'est pas le mien. Just recognize them for now.

", "

Tout, tous, chaque

Tout agrees with the noun that follows, and it comes before the article: tout le magasin, not “le tout magasin”.

FrenchEnglish
masculine singulartout le magasinthe whole shop
feminine singulartoute la journéeall day, the whole day
masculine pluraltous les joursevery day
feminine pluraltoutes les taillesall the sizes

Watch the trap: English “every day” is tous les jours (plural!) and “all day” is toute la journée (singular). Tout alone means “everything”: Tout est en soldes (everything is on sale), C'est tout, merci.

Chaque (each, every) is invariable and always followed by a singular noun with no article: chaque jour, chaque client, chaque semaine. Chaque jour and tous les jours mean almost the same thing.

Tous before a noun has a silent s: tous les jours. On its own, as a pronoun, the s is pronounced: Ils sont tous là (“touss”).

Putting it together

Now combine everything you know: comparatives, object pronouns and demonstratives.

Celle-ci est plus jolie que celle-là, mais elle est plus chère.This one is prettier than that one, but it's more expensive.
Ces chaussures ? Je les ai essayées, mais elles sont trop petites.These shoes? I tried them on, but they're too small.
Je peux l'échanger ? — Oui, avec le ticket de caisse.Can I exchange it? — Yes, with the receipt.
Tous les manteaux sont à moins trente pour cent.All the coats are thirty percent off.
